steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Character: direct/indirect presentation; protagonist/antagonist; character arc

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Narrative perspective: 1st (intimate, biased), 3rd limited (one consciousness), omniscient (all-knowing), stream of consciousness

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Setting: time, place, atmosphere; pathetic fallacy; symbolic settings

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Themes: developed through motifs, recurring images, contrasts, parallels

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Q: Discuss how the first-person narration in 'The Great Gatsby' shapes our understanding of Gatsby --- Solution: Nick as participant-observer creates intimacy but limits access to Gatsby's interiority. His judgement 'Gatsby turned out all right' frames our view. Unreliable moments (drunk at party) and admiration create ambivalence. We see Gatsby through Nick's romanticisation

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Compare 1st vs 3rd person narration effects | Analyse a character foil pair | Discuss symbolic significance of a setting

steps.title: Lesson plan
steps.body: Starter (5 min): Recall prior knowledge of prose and the novel with quick questions. Teaching (15 min): Work through each of the learning objectives, explaining principles step by step. Key points review (5 min): Revisit the key points together, confirming understanding. Worked example (10 min): Model the example question: Discuss how the first-person narration in 'The Great Gatsby' shapes our understanding of Gatsby. Solution: Nick as participant-observer creates intimacy but limits access to Gatsby's interiority. His judgement 'Gatsby turned out all right' frames our view. Unreliable moments (drunk at party) and admiration create ambivalence. We see Gatsby through Nick's romanticisation Practice (10 min): Students attempt the practice questions independently; circulate and support. Plena
